newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian insurance market has huge potential.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian insurance market has huge potential.

text.p: Russia's nascent insurance market offers huge potential but development is being held back by the poor liquidity of insurance companies and the unwillingness of companies to insure themselves.
But however much the market can grow, Russian insurers do not want to see an invasion of Western companies.
"Nothing here is insured," Vladimir Kruglyak, president of Russia's second biggest insurer Ingosstrakh, told Reuters. "Just look out of the window -- there it is and nothing is insured."

Boris Novikov, first deputy chairman of Russia's Federal Insurance Supervision Service (Rosstrakhnadzor), said only seven to eight percent of the market was covered, and the potential for development remained enormous.

On August 1, 1996, there were 3,031 insurance companies registered in Russia with about 2,500 actually operating, Novikov said. The former state domestic monopoly Rosgosstrakh is the biggest with about 15 percent of the market.

In the first half of 1996 Russian insurance companies raised 13.40 trillion roubles in premiums, down from 21.90 trillion in the whole of 1995, according to official statistics, which are not adjusted for inflation nor the depreciation of the rouble.
An insurance analyst, who asked not to be named, said Russian insurance companies did not have enough funds to cover serious risks.
Official statistics say the total authorised capital of Russian insurance companies amounts to 1.50 trillion roubles with insurance reserves of eight trillion.
Companies mostly preferred to insure their employees, which helps them pay less tax, the analyst said.
He also said the market wanted clearer legislation.
Poor risk valuation methods and insufficient funds for technical support also impede the industry, said Andrei Drobinin, chairman of the private ASKO company, which focuses on household insurance.
One of the biggest obstacles is that companies do not fully understand the need for insurance.
"Many businessmen have not yet understood that it is better to pay insurance now than to be left without anything later," Novikov said.
The 1993 fire at truck maker KamAZ, whose main production facility was burnt to the ground, gave a serious push to insurance market development, he said.
"That made many people think," Novikov said. "It is one thing when the state helps state-owned companies, but another when a private company gets burnt."
A new regulation adopted in July on compulsory fire insurance for newly built factories will give further stimulus, he said.
Households represent an easier market for insurance services, but the high inflation rates of the last few years have made long-term insurance saving schemes unprofitable.
In 1992 ASKO provided about 70 percent of the population in Smolensk region with year-long insurance policies, Drobinin said.
Many people did not even bother to turn up to collect their money when the policies matured.
In the early 1990s state-owned Rosgosstrakh started selling pension insurance policies, which were eaten up by inflation.
The government was now discussing the possibility of compensating people for this, Novikov said.
"Psychologically people are ready for insurance," Drobinin said. "They have tried every other financial instrument and next they will try insurance.
"There are possibilities of attracting (funds) and they are big, but it is not because we can offer a lot of products, but because there are very many uninsured individuals."
Rosstrakhnadzor estimates that only about one percent of gross domestic product is spent on insurance in Russia, compared with eight to 10 percent in the West.
But the market is already maturing, and the days of easy profits are over.
The ratio of payments to premiums has risen to 70-80 percent from 20-30 in 1992, said Novikov.
Only about 10 companies have gone bankrupt since 1992, he said.
Foreign involvement in the market is still fairly limited, but growing.
Novikov said only 77 Russian insurance companies had foreign shareholders, including capital from the CIS countries.
"There is more and more interest from foreign companies now," Novikov said. "They are coming."
Foreign presence is impeded by currency laws making it difficult to transfer funds abroad and Russian firms do not welcome competition from abroad.
Russian insurers will not be ready for international competition for at least another five years, said Ingosstrakh's Kruglyak.
"I am against foreign interference into Russia's affairs and I shall fight against it for the rest of my life by absolutely all means," Kruglyak said.

"I am for cooperation with insurers, but we, Russians, will not allow the Russian insurance market to be swallowed by sharks. We shall find a way to hit not only the hands but also the head of those who are crawling into our market." ($1 = 5,423 roubles)
